problem_motivation.content: Extending quantum algorithms to nonlinear mechanics problems is difficult because quantum operations are inherently linear.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: The extension of quantum algorithms to nonlinear problems in mechanics remains challenging due to the inherently linear structure of quantum operations.

problem_motivation.content: Practical realization and multidimensional extension face algorithmic and hardware challenges.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: We discuss several practical algorithmic and hardware-based challenges towards a practical realization of the framework and extension to multi- dimensional problems.

problem_motivation.content: Direct implementation of nonlinear transformations in quantum evaluation is difficult because quantum operations are linear.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: A key challenge, however, arises from the inherently linear nature of quantum operations, which makes the direct implementation of nonlinear transformations involved in the potential energy dif- ficult.

problem_motivation.content: Quantum evaluation of the original energy would have to handle a logarithmic nonlinear term.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: Evaluating (25) within a quantum framework would require us to deal with the logarithmic nonlin- ear term.

problem_motivation.content: The study identifies practical challenges in accuracy, convergence, and computational cost that still need to be addressed.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: The study highlights several practical challenges, including the influence of polynomial approximations on accuracy, convergence difficulties in more complex formulations, and increased computational cost associated with higher-order expansions and auxiliary variables.

problem_motivation.content: There is a need for more efficient approximation strategies that preserve accuracy while reducing quantum resources.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: In particular, developing more efficient approximation strategies that balance accuracy with quantum resource requirements (such as circuit depth and ancilla usage) is of primary interest.

prior_approach.content: Nonlinear mechanics is commonly solved by discretizing to an algebraic system and iteratively solving it.
prior_approach.evidence_span: A common approach to solving nonlinear mechanics problems is to obtain an algebraic system following discretization, which is then solved iteratively.

prior_approach.content: Existing QC work mostly targets linear ODE/PDE problems via quantum linear systems algorithms after discretization.
prior_approach.evidence_span: The majority of the relevant existing QC literature focuses on the evaluation of linear ordinary differential equations (ODEs) and PDEs. A common solution approach is to construct a linear sys- tem of equations following discretization, and evaluating it using quantum linear systems algorithms (QLSAs) [5, 6].

prior_approach.content: HHL introduced a QLSA for sparse linear systems by encoding b and preparing a state proportional to A^{-1}|b⟩.
prior_approach.evidence_span: The foundational work by Harrow et al. [7] (HHL) introduced the first QLSA, which solves sparse linear systems Ax = b by encoding the right-hand side vector b as a quantum state |b⟩. Using Hamiltonian simulation [8] and quantum phase estimation, the algorithm prepares a state |x⟩∝A−1|b⟩ that encodes the properties of the solution vector x.

prior_approach.content: Later QLSA variants used LCU, QSVT, and adiabatic approaches.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Subsequent developments pro- duced high-precision QLSA variants based on linear combination of unitaries (LCU) [9], quantum singular value transformation (QSVT) [10], and adiabatic approaches [11].

prior_approach.content: VQAs use parameterized quantum circuits to evaluate a cost while a classical optimizer updates parameters.
prior_approach.evidence_span: The central idea behind VQAs is to offload the computationally intensive parts of a problem to a quan- tum processor that evaluates a cost function using parameterized quantum circuits encoding the quantity of interest. The circuit parameters are then iteratively updated by a classical optimizer to minimize this cost function.

prior_approach.content: Poisson and elliptic FEM problems have been tackled with QLSAs in the fault-tolerant regime.
prior_approach.evidence_span: For example, the Poisson equation and elliptic finite element problems have been ad- dressed via QLSAs [19, 20], lying in the fault-tolerant quantum computing regime.

prior_approach.content: Liu et al. used a QFT-based algorithm for linear elastic homogenization of periodic composites.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Similarly, Liu et al. [21] demonstrate an algorithm for the linear elastic homogenization of periodic composites using a quantum Fourier transform (QFT)-based approach.

prior_approach.content: VQLS was used for FEM heat conduction and plane-strain elasticity.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Within the VQA regime, the Variational Quantum Linear Solver (VQLS) [22] emerged as one of the prominent VQAs for linear systems, and was used by Arora et al. [23] for FEM-based steady-state heat conduction, and Rao et al. [24] for plane strain elasticity problems.

prior_approach.content: Quantum annealers were used to solve linear finite-element systems via quadratic optimization.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Raisuddin and De [25] instead employed quantum annealers to solve linear finite element systems via an equivalent quadratic optimization formulation.

prior_approach.content: Prior nonlinear quantum approaches reformulate nonlinearities into compatible representations by expanding different quantities.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Several existing approaches refor- mulate nonlinearities in the governing equations into representations compatible with available quantum algorithmic primitives, differing primarily in the quantities being expanded and the re- sulting reformulation.

prior_approach.content: Kyriienko et al. used a truncated Chebyshev quantum feature map and evaluated nonlinear operations classically.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Kyriienko et al. [26] represent the solution function through a truncated Chebyshev quantum feature map, while the nonlinear operations associated with the governing equation are evaluated through classical post-processing.

prior_approach.content: Xu et al. expanded the solution path in a continuation parameter to obtain linear subproblems solved by VQLS.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Xu et al. [27] expand the solution path with respect to a continuation parameter, resulting in a sequence of linear subproblems solved using VQLS.

prior_approach.content: Endo and Takahashi used Carleman linearization to embed a nonlinear differential equation into a larger truncated linear system.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Endo and Takahashi [28] employ Carleman linearization to embed a nonlinear differ- ential equation into a larger truncated linear system.

prior_approach.content: Soize et al. used a related strategy with truncated polynomial expansion for a Fokker–Planck eigenvalue problem solved by VQE.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Soize et al. [29] apply a similar strategy to a Fokker–Planck eigenvalue problem, which, although linear, involves an underlying non-algebraic potential approximated via a truncated polynomial expansion to enable a Variational Quantum Eigensolver-based solution.

prior_approach.content: Lubasch et al. proposed a VQA framework for nonlinear PDEs with polynomial nonlinearities using quantum nonlinear processing units.
prior_approach.evidence_span: In the VQA regime, Lubasch et al. [30, 31] introduced a novel VQA framework for nonlinear PDEs with polynomial nonlinearities by devising quantum nonlinear processing units and demon- strated the efficacy of this approach on Burgers and nonlinear Schr¨odinger equations.

prior_approach.content: Sarma et al. extended the QNPU-based nonlinear PDE approach to a broader class of nonlinear PDEs.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Sarma et al. [32] recently extended this approach to solve a broader class of nonlinear PDEs.

prior_approach.content: These nonlinear PDE VQA works use a least-squares functional as the cost function.
prior_approach.evidence_span: The idea expressed in these works relies on a least-squares functional as the cost function.

prior_approach.content: Sato et al. solved the Poisson equation by minimizing Dirichlet energy in a VQA framework.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Sato et al. [33] proposed a VQA to solve the Poisson equation by formulating the corresponding Dirichlet energy as a cost function parameterized by a quantum circuit.

prior_approach.content: Over and Bengoechea et al. derived a variational form for the time-discrete advection–diffusion equation and minimized it with VQA.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Similarly, Over and Bengoechea et al. [34, 35], also derived a variational form for the advection–diffusion equation in the time-discrete setting and minimized it within a VQA framework.

prior_limitation.content: QLSA-style methods need deep circuits and low error rates beyond NISQ hardware capabilities.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: However, despite their favorable asymptotic complexity, the aforementioned approaches require deep circuits and error rates that are beyond the capabilities of the NISQ-era hardware [12].

prior_limitation.content: VQAs suffer trainability issues such as barren plateaus, especially with larger width/depth.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: VQAs face well-documented trainability challenges. As circuit width or ansatz depth increases, the cost landscape can develop barren plateaus, regions where gradients vanish exponentially and classical optimization stalls [16]

prior_limitation.content: Existing methods for nonlinear transformations can be resource-intensive.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: Existing methods for nonlinear transformations can be resource-intensive [42].

prior_limitation.content: Arbitrary quantum-state preparation is a bottleneck whose complexity scales exponentially with qubit count.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: Preparation of arbitrary quantum states is a well- known bottleneck in quantum computing. The complexity to prepare an arbitrary state scales exponentially with number of qubits [54].

prior_limitation.content: Current implementations are limited by expensive statevector simulation, especially for larger problems, which prevents scaling analysis.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: In addition, current implementations are limited by the cost of statevector simulations, particularly for larger problem sizes, restricting the analysis of scaling behavior.

rejected_alternative.content: The work uses minimization of the variational form rather than the weak form to make the problem suitable for VQA.
rejected_alternative.evidence_span: (1) The numerical problem is expressed as the minimization of the variational form (as opposed to the weak form) to prepare it for VQA;

rejected_alternative.content: Instead of resource-intensive nonlinear-transformation methods, the paper uses low-degree polynomial approximations implemented by shallow QNPU circuits for NISQ suitability.
rejected_alternative.evidence_span: Instead, we propose low-degree polynomial approximations of arbitrary nonlinearities, which can be imple- mented using relatively shallow quantum circuits known as Quantum Nonlinear Processing Units (QNPUs), as developed in [30], and are more suitable for near-term NISQ devices.

rejected_alternative.content: The study simplifies the compressible Neo-Hookean model by setting Λ=0 and using a 1D unidirectional representation.
rejected_alternative.evidence_span: For the present study, we consider a special case of the compressible Neo-Hookean model by setting Λ = 0, which eliminates the volumetric resistance term, and focusing on a unidirectional and one-dimensional representation.

rejected_alternative.content: Taylor expansion is preferred when small loads keep u′ within its validity range; IHT is reserved for larger deformations because it is costlier to implement.
rejected_alternative.evidence_span: Although more flexible than the Taylor series, the IHT expansion is costlier to implement within the current framework, requiring the auxiliary variable and penalty formulation introduced below. Consequently, the Taylor expansion is preferred whenever small enough loadings keep u′ within its range of validity, with the IHT expansion reserved for larger deformations.

hypothesis_statement.content: A variational quantum formulation can solve nonlinear elasticity problems from hyperelastic models using a hybrid quantum-classical approach.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: This manuscript explores a variational quantum formulation for nonlinear elasticity problems arising from hyperelastic material models. The approach leverages the potential energy structure of hyperelasticity and employs a hybrid quantum–classical framework

hypothesis_statement.content: The proposed framework uses hyperelastic strain-energy structure to formulate nonlinear elasticity as a variational quantum problem.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: This manuscript presents a VQA-based approach for nonlinear elasticity problems arising from hyperelastic material models under certain assumptions. The proposed framework exploits the fact that, for hyperelastic materials, the stress is derived from a strain energy density function, thereby enabling a variational formulation in terms of a total potential energy functional [36, 37, 38, 39, 40]. The resulting approximated potential energy functional is constructed to integrate naturally within a variational quantum framework.

hypothesis_statement.content: A complete VQA framework can be built by encoding the displacement field as a quantum state and using potential energy as the cost function.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: The VQA framework requires a cost function to optimize, which we construct from the system’s potential energy. To evaluate this energy on a quantum 3 computer, the displacement field (represented by its discretized values) must be encoded as a quantum state. This motivates the introduction of a quantum representation of real-valued vectors. Finally, we integrate these components to establish a complete framework for approximating the solution to the underlying elasticity problem.

evidence_result.content: Numerical experiments show that the proposed method is feasible for near-term quantum devices while examining how polynomial order affects accuracy and efficiency.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Numerical experiments investigate the influence of the polynomial approximation order on the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed approach, illustrating its feasibility for near-term quantum devices.

evidence_result.content: The method is demonstrated on a simplified one-dimensional Neo-Hookean problem, with two approximation strategies and evaluation of polynomial-order effects.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The proposed methodology is demonstrated on a simplified one-dimensional Neo-Hookean material-based problem. Two distinct approximation strategies are developed and implemented in accordance with contemporary VQA capabilities. The displacement field is discretized using first- and second-order finite element shape functions, and the formulation accommodates nonhomogeneous boundary conditions. The influence of higher-order polynomial approximations on the efficiency and accuracy of the VQA implementation is evaluated.

evidence_result.content: The proposed VQA framework was demonstrated on a 1D Neo-Hookean case and reproduced expected behavior with first- and second-order finite elements on non-uniform meshes and non-homogeneous boundary conditions.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The methodology was demonstrated on a special case of one-dimensional Neo-Hookean problem, where the potential energy functional is used as the VQA cost function. Two types of polynomial approximations were investigated, and the VQA was shown to capture the expected behavior using both first- and second-order finite element discretizations on non-uniform meshes with non-homogeneous boundary conditions.

problem_motivation.content: A core motivation/problem is that extending quantum algorithms to nonlinear mechanics/energy evaluation is difficult because quantum operations are inherently linear, making direct implementation of nonlinear transformations—such as the logarithmic nonlinear term in the original energy—challenging.
evidence_spans: The extension of quantum algorithms to nonlinear problems in mechanics remains challenging due to the inherently linear structure of quantum operations.

A key challenge, however, arises from the inherently linear nature of quantum operations, which makes the direct implementation of nonlinear transformations involved in the potential energy dif- ficult.
Evaluating (25) within a quantum framework would require us to deal with the logarithmic nonlin- ear term.

problem_motivation.content: Beyond the core nonlinearity issue, practical deployment and scaling of the framework face algorithmic and hardware challenges, including multidimensional extension, accuracy and convergence limitations from polynomial approximations, increased computational cost from higher-order expansions and auxiliary variables, and the need for more resource-efficient approximation strategies that preserve accuracy while reducing circuit depth and ancilla usage.
evidence_spans: We discuss several practical algorithmic and hardware-based challenges towards a practical realization of the framework and extension to multi- dimensional problems.

The study highlights several practical challenges, including the influence of polynomial approximations on accuracy, convergence difficulties in more complex formulations, and increased computational cost associated with higher-order expansions and auxiliary variables.
In particular, developing more efficient approximation strategies that balance accuracy with quantum resource requirements (such as circuit depth and ancilla usage) is of primary interest.

prior_approach.content: A common classical approach for nonlinear mechanics is to discretize the governing equations into an algebraic system and solve it iteratively.
evidence_spans: A common approach to solving nonlinear mechanics problems is to obtain an algebraic system following discretization, which is then solved iteratively.

prior_approach.content: Most prior quantum computing work for mechanics/PDEs has focused on linear ODE/PDE problems after discretization, typically constructing a linear system and solving it with quantum linear systems algorithms (QLSAs).
evidence_spans: The majority of the relevant existing QC literature focuses on the evaluation of linear ordinary differential equations (ODEs) and PDEs. A common solution approach is to construct a linear sys- tem of equations following discretization, and evaluating it using quantum linear systems algorithms (QLSAs) [5, 6].

prior_approach.content: Foundational and subsequent QLSA-based prior work includes HHL for sparse linear systems, which encodes |b⟩ and prepares a state proportional to A^{-1}|b⟩ using Hamiltonian simulation and phase estimation, followed by later high-precision variants based on LCU, QSVT, and adiabatic methods.
evidence_spans: The foundational work by Harrow et al. [7] (HHL) introduced the first QLSA, which solves sparse linear systems Ax = b by encoding the right-hand side vector b as a quantum state |b⟩. Using Hamiltonian simulation [8] and quantum phase estimation, the algorithm prepares a state |x⟩∝A−1|b⟩ that encodes the properties of the solution vector x.
Subsequent developments pro- duced high-precision QLSA variants based on linear combination of unitaries (LCU) [9], quantum singular value transformation (QSVT) [10], and adiabatic approaches [11].

prior_approach.content: QLSA-based applications in computational mechanics/scientific computing include fault-tolerant quantum algorithms for the Poisson equation and elliptic finite-element problems, and a QFT-based algorithm for linear elastic homogenization of periodic composites.
evidence_spans: For example, the Poisson equation and elliptic finite element problems have been ad- dressed via QLSAs [19, 20], lying in the fault-tolerant quantum computing regime.
Similarly, Liu et al. [21] demonstrate an algorithm for the linear elastic homogenization of periodic composites using a quantum Fourier transform (QFT)-based approach.

prior_approach.content: Variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) are a prior approach in which a parameterized quantum circuit evaluates a cost function and a classical optimizer iteratively updates the circuit parameters.
evidence_spans: The central idea behind VQAs is to offload the computationally intensive parts of a problem to a quan- tum processor that evaluates a cost function using parameterized quantum circuits encoding the quantity of interest. The circuit parameters are then iteratively updated by a classical optimizer to minimize this cost function.

prior_approach.content: Within the VQA regime, the Variational Quantum Linear Solver (VQLS) has been used for linear finite-element applications including steady-state heat conduction and plane-strain elasticity.
evidence_spans: Within the VQA regime, the Variational Quantum Linear Solver (VQLS) [22] emerged as one of the prominent VQAs for linear systems, and was used by Arora et al. [23] for FEM-based steady-state heat conduction, and Rao et al. [24] for plane strain elasticity problems.

prior_approach.content: Quantum annealers have also been used as a prior approach for linear finite-element systems by reformulating them as equivalent quadratic optimization problems.
evidence_spans: Raisuddin and De [25] instead employed quantum annealers to solve linear finite element systems via an equivalent quadratic optimization formulation.

prior_approach.content: Prior quantum approaches for nonlinear problems often reformulate nonlinearities into forms compatible with quantum primitives, differing mainly in what quantity is expanded and the resulting reformulation.
evidence_spans: Several existing approaches refor- mulate nonlinearities in the governing equations into representations compatible with available quantum algorithmic primitives, differing primarily in the quantities being expanded and the re- sulting reformulation.

prior_approach.content: Examples of prior nonlinear reformulation strategies include: representing the solution via a truncated Chebyshev quantum feature map while evaluating nonlinear operations classically; expanding the solution path in a continuation parameter to obtain a sequence of linear subproblems solved by VQLS; using Carleman linearization to embed a nonlinear differential equation into a larger truncated linear system; and using a related truncated polynomial expansion for a Fokker–Planck eigenvalue problem solved by VQE.
evidence_spans: Kyriienko et al. [26] represent the solution function through a truncated Chebyshev quantum feature map, while the nonlinear operations associated with the governing equation are evaluated through classical post-processing.
Xu et al. [27] expand the solution path with respect to a continuation parameter, resulting in a sequence of linear subproblems solved using VQLS.
Endo and Takahashi [28] employ Carleman linearization to embed a nonlinear differ- ential equation into a larger truncated linear system.

Soize et al. [29] apply a similar strategy to a Fokker–Planck eigenvalue problem, which, although linear, involves an underlying non-algebraic potential approximated via a truncated polynomial expansion to enable a Variational Quantum Eigensolver-based solution.

prior_approach.content: A distinct prior VQA line for nonlinear PDEs was introduced by Lubasch et al., who proposed quantum nonlinear processing units (QNPUs) for polynomial nonlinearities and demonstrated them on Burgers and nonlinear Schrödinger equations; Sarma et al. later extended this approach to a broader class of nonlinear PDEs. These works use a least-squares functional as the cost function.
evidence_spans: In the VQA regime, Lubasch et al. [30, 31] introduced a novel VQA framework for nonlinear PDEs with polynomial nonlinearities by devising quantum nonlinear processing units and demon- strated the efficacy of this approach on Burgers and nonlinear Schr¨odinger equations.
Sarma et al. [32] recently extended this approach to solve a broader class of nonlinear PDEs.
The idea expressed in these works relies on a least-squares functional as the cost function.

prior_approach.content: Another prior variational line formulates PDE solving as minimizing an energy or variational functional in a VQA framework, including minimizing Dirichlet energy for the Poisson equation and minimizing a derived variational form for the time-discrete advection–diffusion equation.
evidence_spans: Sato et al. [33] proposed a VQA to solve the Poisson equation by formulating the corresponding Dirichlet energy as a cost function parameterized by a quantum circuit.
Similarly, Over and Bengoechea et al. [34, 35], also derived a variational form for the advection–diffusion equation in the time-discrete setting and minimized it within a VQA framework.

hypothesis_statement.content: The paper hypothesizes that nonlinear elasticity problems for hyperelastic materials can be cast and approximately solved within a hybrid quantum-classical variational quantum algorithm framework by exploiting the hyperelastic strain-energy / total potential energy structure, encoding the displacement field as a quantum state, and using the (approximated) potential energy as the VQA cost function.
evidence_spans: This manuscript explores a variational quantum formulation for nonlinear elasticity problems arising from hyperelastic material models. The approach leverages the potential energy structure of hyperelasticity and employs a hybrid quantum–classical framework

This manuscript presents a VQA-based approach for nonlinear elasticity problems arising from hyperelastic material models under certain assumptions. The proposed framework exploits the fact that, for hyperelastic materials, the stress is derived from a strain energy density function, thereby enabling a variational formulation in terms of a total potential energy functional [36, 37, 38, 39, 40]. The resulting approximated potential energy functional is constructed to integrate naturally within a variational quantum framework.

The VQA framework requires a cost function to optimize, which we construct from the system’s potential energy. To evaluate this energy on a quantum 3 computer, the displacement field (represented by its discretized values) must be encoded as a quantum state. This motivates the introduction of a quantum representation of real-valued vectors. Finally, we integrate these components to establish a complete framework for approximating the solution to the underlying elasticity problem.

hypothesis_statement.content: The paper further hypothesizes that nonlinear terms in the energy can be made compatible with the VQA by approximating them with truncated polynomials, thereby defining an approximated potential-energy cost function; alternatively, a constrained reformulation with an auxiliary variable z may avoid approximating the logarithmic term while preserving polynomial nonlinearities.

evidence_result.content: The proposed VQA framework was demonstrated on a simplified one-dimensional Neo-Hookean problem, using two polynomial approximation strategies, first- and second-order finite element discretizations, and accommodating non-uniform meshes and non-homogeneous boundary conditions; it reproduced the expected behavior.
evidence_spans: The proposed methodology is demonstrated on a simplified one-dimensional Neo-Hookean material-based problem. Two distinct approximation strategies are developed and implemented in accordance with contemporary VQA capabilities. The displacement field is discretized using first- and second-order finite element shape functions, and the formulation accommodates nonhomogeneous boundary conditions.

The methodology was demonstrated on a special case of one-dimensional Neo-Hookean problem, where the potential energy functional is used as the VQA cost function. Two types of polynomial approximations were investigated, and the VQA was shown to capture the expected behavior using both first- and second-order finite element discretizations on non-uniform meshes with non-homogeneous boundary conditions.

constraint.content: Scalability and practical deployment remain unresolved constraints: extension beyond the current 1D proof-of-concept to realistic 2D/3D hyperelastic problems is future work, and real-hardware use must cope with noise, coupling latency, native-gate-set compilation, and cloud queue times through hardware-aware optimization.
evidence_spans: The present 1D study establishes the feasibility of the proposed formulations in a controlled proof-of-concept setting, while their computational scalability and efficient extension to realistic 2D and 3D hyperelastic problems remain subjects for future investigation.

The impact of hardware noise, cou-pling latency, native-gate-set compilation, and cloud-access queue times on the performance of the framework when deployed on real hardware requires further optimization of algorithmic choices and efficient hardware-aware implementation.
